MTU per hop.tag: The biggest packet that reaches each hop.
MTU per hop.what: Traces the path, then sends Don't-Fragment pings with a rising TTL and finds the biggest size each hop still passes - about 8 small pings per hop, fewer after the first.
MTU per hop.why: Where the size drops is where your packets get wrapped (PPPoE, a VPN, a tunnel) - and a silent drop (black hole) is why pages half-load or VPNs stall.

MTU over UDP (QUIC / DNS).tag: The biggest UDP packet that gets through - even where ping is blocked
MTU over UDP (QUIC / DNS).what: Finds the largest UDP packet that reaches a QUIC web server (port 443) or a DNS server (port 53) and gets an answer, with don't-fragment set. Useful on VPNs and company networks that drop ping, and for the UDP traffic itself: HTTP/3, calls, games.
MTU over UDP (QUIC / DNS).how: Port 443: a QUIC packet with an unused version number - QUIC servers answer it with the versions they speak, and no connection is made. Port 53: a DNS question for the root, padded to the size being tried. About 12 sizes, two tries each, to the one target you typed.
MTU over UDP (QUIC / DNS).why: When UDP packets above a size vanish (a VPN or tunnel that doesn't fit them), HTTP/3 sites stall and VPNs misbehave while ping-based MTU checks look fine - or can't run at all because ping is blocked.

labels.Biggest UDP packet through|0: Full size for a tunnel-free line - nothing on the way shrinks UDP.

MTR - loss per hop over time.tag: Loss and delay at every hop, over minutes.
MTR - loss per hop over time.what: One probe per hop per second for as long as you choose, then reads it the way engineers do.
MTR - loss per hop over time.why: Loss at a middle hop that doesn't carry on to the end is just that router ignoring pings - only loss that continues is real.

The way back (return path).tag: As much of the return path as one PC can know.
The way back (return path).what: Reads the TTL every reply arrives with (how many routers it crossed on the way back), asks routers to write their addresses into the packet (Record Route), and - with online lookups on - shows how other networks reach you.
The way back (return path).why: Slowness or loss is often only on the way back; a different number of hops back than out means a different road.

Who carries my traffic (BGP).tag: Every network on your path, by name.
Who carries my traffic (BGP).what: Traces the path, then asks RIPEstat which network (AS) owns each public hop, where they hand over (PeeringDB internet exchanges), the destination's route, its RPKI status and recent route changes.
Who carries my traffic (BGP).why: Tells you which company adds the delay - your provider, a carrier, or the destination.

Which route does this take?.what: Asks Windows for the route it picks for a destination: the adapter, the next hop, the route that matched and its metric.
Which route does this take?.why: Answers 'does this go into the VPN or out the home internet?' - split tunnels and overlapping routes.

Your gateway and failover.tag: Is your gateway one router or a redundant pair?
Your gateway and failover.what: Reads the gateway's MAC address: a VRRP, HSRP or GLBP virtual address means two or more routers share it. Watches it every 30 s and notes a takeover.
Your gateway and failover.why: A short outage with a MAC change at the same minute is a router failover, not your PC. Also shows slow plug-in (spanning tree).

IPv6 routers on this network.what: Lists the routers and prefixes Windows learned from router advertisements on each network.
IPv6 routers on this network.why: Two IPv6 routers on a home or office LAN is often a rogue device - traffic may go to it.

Routing protocols on my segment.tag: What routers say on your network.
Routing protocols on my segment.what: Listens (with Wireshark + Npcap) for OSPF, EIGRP, RIP, IS-IS, PIM, LDP, BFD, VRRP, HSRP, IPv6 RAs, DHCP servers, spanning tree, LLDP / CDP, DTP. Nothing sent, nothing saved.
Routing protocols on my segment.why: Routing hellos on a user segment mean the router interface isn't passive - a security finding. Two DHCP servers or RA senders mean a rogue device.

labels.OSPF hello|3: A router is offering OSPF to anything on this segment - usually only routers should be here.

Announcements (mDNS, SSDP, LLMNR, NetBIO.tag: Devices and names announced on your network.
Announcements (mDNS, SSDP, LLMNR, NetBIO.what: Listens for mDNS (Bonjour), SSDP / UPnP, LLMNR and NetBIOS - which devices announce themselves and which names they ask for.
Announcements (mDNS, SSDP, LLMNR, NetBIO.how: Needs Wireshark + Npcap; listens only, sends nothing, saves nothing.
Announcements (mDNS, SSDP, LLMNR, NetBIO.why: Finds printers, TVs and smart devices - and the old LLMNR / NetBIOS lookups that let a device on the segment answer falsely and collect sign-in hashes.

IPv6 ping and trace.tag: Does IPv6 work all the way?
IPv6 ping and trace.what: Pings and traces a destination over IPv6 only, using Windows' own IPv6 echo (no admin).
IPv6 ping and trace.why: Broken IPv6 makes apps wait before falling back to IPv4; this shows where it breaks.

Overlapping networks (home vs VPN).tag: Your home network and the VPN using the same addresses.
Overlapping networks (home vs VPN).what: Compares the address ranges of every active adapter and the VPN's routes.
Overlapping networks (home vs VPN).why: The classic 'works in the office, not at home over VPN': a company server in the same range as your home network is unreachable.

labels.Overlap|1: While the VPN is on, company addresses 10.0.0.x go to your home network instead. Ask IT for a narrower route, or change the home network to e.g. 192.168.50.0/24.

IPv6 vs IPv4.what: Opens one connection over each to the same site and compares.
IPv6 vs IPv4.why: Broken IPv6 makes every site wait a moment before falling back to IPv4.

VPN and company proxy - is it the slow p.tag: Is the VPN the slow part?
VPN and company proxy - is it the slow p.what: Recognises the common VPN and zero-trust clients (GlobalProtect, Cisco Secure Client, Zscaler, Netskope, FortiClient, Ivanti, Check Point, Cloudflare WARP, Tailscale, WireGuard, OpenVPN, NordVPN, Proton and more), says whether everything goes through the tunnel or only company traffic, shows any proxy or PAC script - and times the tunnel as its own layer: router, the VPN's far side, then the whole
VPN and company proxy - is it the slow p.how: Reads the running program names, the network adapters and Windows' proxy settings - nothing is changed. The only packets are 7 pings (or timed connections to port 53) to the VPN's own DNS server.
VPN and company proxy - is it the slow p.why: "The internet is slow" on a work laptop is very often the VPN: a full tunnel sends every site to the company first. Knowing the tunnel's own share tells you whether to pick a nearer gateway, ask IT about split tunnelling, or look elsewhere.

Which proxy does this URL use?.tag: Direct, a proxy or a PAC script - for this exact URL.
Which proxy does this URL use?.what: Asks Windows the same question your browser asks, and reads the WinHTTP setting background services use.
Which proxy does this URL use?.why: Sites that fail only on one PC or only in the browser are often a proxy rule.

Hosts file.tag: Names pinned to a fixed address on this PC.
Hosts file.why: An old line there breaks a site only on this PC.

DNS hijack and VPN name rules.tag: Does your DNS tell the truth, and who answers company names?
DNS hijack and VPN name rules.what: Looks up one made-up name, and reads the name rules (NRPT) your VPN or IT set.
DNS hijack and VPN name rules.why: A provider that answers made-up names sends typos to its ad page; missing VPN rules send company names to the wrong DNS.

Port test.what: Opens one TCP connection with a 4-second limit.
Port test.why: Refused = the server said no; no answer = a firewall silently dropped it.

Teams UDP test (and NAT type).tag: Can Teams calls use UDP here?
Teams UDP test (and NAT type).what: Sends one STUN request to Microsoft's Teams relays on UDP 3478 and reads how your NAT maps it.
Teams UDP test (and NAT type).why: Without UDP, calls are squeezed into TCP 443 and stutter; a symmetric NAT forces every call through a relay.

Clock check.what: Compares your clock with the time in one answer from msftconnecttest.com (the page Windows itself uses).
Clock check.why: More than about 5 minutes off breaks certificates and company sign-in.

iperf3 to your server.tag: Real throughput to your own server.
iperf3 to your server.what: Speaks the iperf3 protocol to an iperf3 server you run (iperf3 -s): TCP up, down or both, several streams, or UDP at a set rate with jitter and loss.
iperf3 to your server.why: The honest number for Wi-Fi, a VPN or a link - not a speed-test website's.

Latency under load (bufferbloat).tag: Does your line stay quick when it's full?
Latency under load (bufferbloat).what: Pings while your own iperf3 server fills the line - first downloading, then uploading - and grades how much the delay grows (A+ to F, the scale speed-test sites use).
Latency under load (bufferbloat).how: About 30 seconds of real traffic to the iperf3 server you name, plus 4 pings a second to the ping target.
Latency under load (bufferbloat).why: Bufferbloat is why calls and games stutter when someone else uploads photos - the speed test looks fine but the delay balloons.

labels.Grade|2: Calls and games stutter while someone uploads. Turn on SQM / Smart Queue on the router (set to about 90% of your speed).

Sustained ping.what: Hundreds of pings at the interval you choose, drawn as a timeline with losses in red, plus jitter and the longest gap.
Sustained ping.why: Bursts of loss point at Wi-Fi or a flapping link; steady loss at a busy line.

DSCP-marked ping.tag: Does a priority marking change anything?
DSCP-marked ping.what: Pings the target with a DSCP marking (EF for voice, AF41 for video, CS6...) and unmarked in turn, and compares delay and loss.
DSCP-marked ping.how: Alternating marked and unmarked pings, two a second.
DSCP-marked ping.why: Checks whether the network polices or prioritises a class - for example voice traffic that gets dropped once it's marked.

TCP ping.tag: Ping that works where ping is blocked.
TCP ping.what: Opens and closes a TCP connection to host:port once a second and times the handshake.
TCP ping.why: Firewalls often drop ping (ICMP) but let TCP through - and TCP is what apps actually use.

TWAMP-light to a reflector.tag: Loss and jitter each way, to a reflector.
TWAMP-light to a reflector.what: Sends numbered, timestamped UDP packets to a TWAMP-light reflector (port 862 by default), which stamps and returns them.
TWAMP-light to a reflector.why: Tells loss on the way out from loss on the way back, and jitter per direction - what ping can't.

Nearest cloud.tag: How far Microsoft 365, Google and the big clouds are from you.
Nearest cloud.what: Times a connection to each front door.
Nearest cloud.why: Microsoft 365 far away means your traffic leaves through a VPN or proxy in another city.

dig - any DNS record.tag: Any DNS record, from any server - or follow the delegation.
dig - any DNS record.what: Asks the DNS server directly (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, CNAME, SOA, SRV, CAA, PTR). TRACE starts at a root server and follows each referral down to the domain's own server.
dig - any DNS record.why: Shows the TTL, who answered, and whether DNSSEC validated.

HTTP and TLS inspector.what: Follows the redirect chain, lists the useful headers (HSTS, HTTP/3 offered, caches), tries TLS 1.3 and 1.2, and reads the certificate: names, expiry, issuer, inspected or not.
HTTP and TLS inspector.why: The quick answer to 'why does the browser complain about this site'.

HTTP timing, repeated.tag: Where a slow website spends its time.
HTTP timing, repeated.what: Fetches a URL several times and splits each into name lookup, connect, TLS, first byte and download - like curl -w.
HTTP timing, repeated.why: The spread of each step points at DNS, distance, the server or bandwidth.

Encrypted DNS (DoH / DoT).tag: Do DoH and DoT get through?
Encrypted DNS (DoH / DoT).what: Asks Cloudflare and Google over DNS-over-HTTPS, and 1.1.1.1 over DNS-over-TLS (TCP 853), for example.com.
Encrypted DNS (DoH / DoT).why: Browsers fall back silently when encrypted DNS is blocked; this shows what your network allows.

NTP - ask a time server.what: Sends one SNTP v4 request and reads stratum, reference, round trip and how far your clock is off.
NTP - ask a time server.why: Checks a company or public NTP server is reachable and sane, and how wrong this PC's clock is.

Mail server (SMTP / IMAP / POP).tag: Is the mail server talking, and securely?
Mail server (SMTP / IMAP / POP).what: Reads the greeting and what the server offers (EHLO / CAPABILITY / CAPA), tries STARTTLS and reads the certificate. Never logs in.
Mail server (SMTP / IMAP / POP).why: Tells blocked port, wrong port, missing STARTTLS or an expired certificate apart.

SSH banner.tag: Is SSH there, and which one?
SSH banner.what: Connects and reads the version line the SSH server sends first. Never logs in.
SSH banner.why: Shows the port is open and what software answers (OpenSSH, a router's SSH...).

SNMP - what is this device?.tag: Ask a device who it is.
SNMP - what is this device?.what: Reads its name, description, uptime, location, contact and product ID over SNMP v2c or v3 (no auth, auth, or auth + AES privacy).
SNMP - what is this device?.why: Confirms SNMP, the credentials and the access list all work from this PC.

SNMP - interfaces (status, errors).tag: Which ports are down, and which have errors.
SNMP - interfaces (status, errors).what: Reads the interfaces table (IF-MIB): name, admin and operational state, speed, errors and discards, description - problems first.
SNMP - interfaces (status, errors).why: Admin up but down is a cable, optic or far-end problem; growing errors point at a bad cable, optic or duplex mismatch.

labels.Port 7|2: A bad cable or dirty optic - swap the patch lead first.

SNMP - traffic per port.tag: How busy each port is right now.
SNMP - traffic per port.what: Reads the 64-bit traffic counters twice, 5 seconds apart, and shows the rate per port - busiest first, with the share of its speed.
SNMP - traffic per port.why: A port near 100% of its speed is the bottleneck.

SNMP - CPU and memory.what: Reads processor load and memory / storage use from the standard HOST-RESOURCES-MIB.
SNMP - CPU and memory.why: A device at 100% CPU drops control traffic and answers slowly.

SNMP - neighbours (LLDP).tag: Who is plugged into which port.
SNMP - neighbours (LLDP).what: Reads the LLDP neighbour table: our port, the neighbour's name, its port and chassis.
SNMP - neighbours (LLDP).why: Confirms cabling without walking to the rack.

SNMP - sensors (temperature, optics).what: Reads the standard sensor table (ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB) with names, scaled values and state - problems first.
SNMP - sensors (temperature, optics).why: A hot device or a weak optic (low dBm) explains errors and drops.

SNMP - device snapshot (everything at on.tag: Overview, ports, CPU, sensors, neighbours at once.
SNMP - device snapshot (everything at on.what: Runs the overview, interfaces, CPU and memory, sensors and LLDP views one after another, with one time limit, into one result you can copy or save.
SNMP - device snapshot (everything at on.how: Read-only GET / GETBULK, the same as each view on its own; stops at 3 minutes.
SNMP - device snapshot (everything at on.why: One record of a device's state before and after a change, or to attach to a ticket.

SNMP - find a MAC on a switch.tag: Which switch port a device is on.
SNMP - find a MAC on a switch.what: Looks up a MAC (or an IP, through the device's ARP table) in the switch's forwarding table (BRIDGE-MIB / Q-BRIDGE-MIB) and names the port. Empty lists the whole table, busiest ports first.
SNMP - find a MAC on a switch.how: Read-only walks of the forwarding table and the bridge-port to interface map.
SNMP - find a MAC on a switch.why: Finding where a device is plugged in without tracing cables. A port with many MACs is an uplink - follow it to the next switch.

SNMP - VLANs and their ports.what: Reads the VLAN table (Q-BRIDGE-MIB): each VLAN's name, its untagged and tagged ports, and each port's native VLAN (PVID). Older Cisco switches are read from their VTP table.
SNMP - VLANs and their ports.how: Read-only walks; port lists are decoded from the switch's bitmaps.
SNMP - VLANs and their ports.why: A device in the wrong VLAN gets the wrong addresses or none - this shows which VLAN each port really carries.

SNMP - PoE power per port.what: Reads POWER-ETHERNET-MIB: the switch's power budget and use, and each port's state (off, searching, powering, fault) and class - faults first.
SNMP - PoE power per port.why: A phone or access point that won't start is often a PoE fault or an exhausted power budget.

SNMP - link aggregation (LACP).tag: Is every LAG member in its bundle?
SNMP - link aggregation (LACP).what: Reads the LACP table (IEEE8023-LAG-MIB): each member's bundle, whether it's in sync, collecting and distributing, and its partner - a member cabled to a different switch stands out. Without LACP it reads the interface stack.
SNMP - link aggregation (LACP).why: A member that dropped out halves the bandwidth silently; a mis-cabled one can loop or black-hole traffic.

SNMP - printer status and toner.what: Reads the Printer MIB: idle / printing, error flags (jam, door open, no paper, toner), supply levels, what the panel says, page count and alerts.
SNMP - printer status and toner.how: Read-only; most printers answer the community public.
SNMP - printer status and toner.why: Tells you why a printer isn't printing without walking to it.

SNMP - UPS battery and runtime.what: Reads UPS-MIB (or APC's own MIB): whether it's on mains or battery, battery state and charge, minutes of runtime left, load and alarms.
SNMP - UPS battery and runtime.why: Know before an outage whether the UPS will actually carry the network gear.

SNMP - walk any OID or name.tag: Any table, rebuilt so you can read it.
SNMP - walk any OID or name.what: Walks an OID or a name from your MIBs (GETBULK, up to 2,000 values), names every column, decodes the values and joins columns into rows - admin-up-but-down rows first.
SNMP - walk any OID or name.why: Turns hundreds of numbered lines into one readable table.

MIB folder and search.tag: Find the right object before you query.
MIB folder and search.what: Lists your MIB folder and searches every object's name and description - click a result to walk it on the device.
MIB folder and search.why: No more guessing OIDs: search 'temperature' or 'optic' and walk what it finds.

Syslog - send a test message.tag: Send one test message to a collector.
Syslog - send a test message.what: Sends one RFC 5424 message over UDP 514 (or your port).
Syslog - send a test message.why: Checks a firewall or collector filter - look for the message on the collector.

ICMP builder (size, DF, TTL).tag: Ping with your own size, DF, TTL and gap.
ICMP builder (size, DF, TTL).what: Sends ping (ICMP echo) to one target with the size, don't-fragment flag, TTL, count and gap you choose - IPv4 or IPv6 - and reports answers, loss, packet-too-big and which router answered when the TTL ran out.
ICMP builder (size, DF, TTL).how: Windows' own ping API; no admin. At most 10 a second and 1,000 in all.
ICMP builder (size, DF, TTL).why: Prove an MTU problem (size + df), find the hop where a TTL runs out, or check a firewall rule for ICMP.

UDP sender.tag: Your own UDP payload to host:port.
UDP sender.what: Sends a text or hex payload to one UDP port up to 1,000 times (10 a second at most) and shows any answer, or that the port is closed.
UDP sender.why: Test a firewall rule, a SIP / syslog / custom service, or that a port-forward reaches the box.

TCP sender (send, see the reply).what: Connects to host:port, sends what you typed (text with \r\n, or hex) and shows up to 4 KB of the reply.
TCP sender (send, see the reply).how: An ordinary TCP connection, closed after 3 seconds.
TCP sender (send, see the reply).why: Talk to a service by hand - an HTTP line, a banner, a custom protocol - like telnet or netcat.

ARP who-has.tag: Who has this IP on my LAN?
ARP who-has.what: Asks Windows to send one ARP request for an address on your own subnet and shows the MAC that answered and how fast.
ARP who-has.why: Find a device's MAC, or spot two devices claiming the same IP.

DHCP options from the server.tag: What the DHCP server hands out.
DHCP options from the server.what: Asks your DHCP server (a DHCP information request, through Windows) for its options: router, DNS, domain, NTP, TFTP / boot file, classless routes, WPAD and vendor options.
DHCP options from the server.how: Windows' DHCP client API; your address and lease are not touched.
DHCP options from the server.why: Phones and APs that fetch config by TFTP, wrong DNS or NTP from DHCP, or a WPAD proxy you didn't expect.

SNMP test trap (send only).tag: Does my trap receiver see this?
SNMP test trap (send only).what: Sends one SNMPv2c notification (Net-SNMP's heartbeat test OID) with a text saying it's a test, to your trap receiver.
SNMP test trap (send only).how: One UDP packet to port 162; AdeeboMeter never receives traps or changes a device.
SNMP test trap (send only).why: Prove the path, firewall and community to your NMS before trusting it to alert you.

NetFlow test record.what: Sends one NetFlow v5 packet with one flow from this PC to a documentation address (192.0.2.10), so you can find it on the collector.
NetFlow test record.why: Check the collector's port, firewall and parsing before pointing routers at it.

HTTP request builder.what: Sends one HTTP request with the method, headers and body you choose and shows the status, time, every response header and the start of the body. Redirects are shown, not followed.
HTTP request builder.how: Through your proxy settings, like a browser; 15 s limit, 64 KB read.
HTTP request builder.why: Test an API, a health check, a POST to a webhook, or what a server says to OPTIONS - without curl or Postman.

STUN - my public address and port.what: Sends a STUN binding request to the server you name and shows the address and port the internet sees, and whether your NAT kept the port.
STUN - my public address and port.why: Calls and VoIP depend on how NAT maps ports; this shows it directly.

Name of a device (NetBIOS, LLMNR, mDNS).what: Asks that one device for its name over NetBIOS (with its workgroup and MAC), LLMNR and mDNS (Bonjour), and your DNS server for a PTR name.
Name of a device (NetBIOS, LLMNR, mDNS).how: A few small UDP questions to that one IP.
Name of a device (NetBIOS, LLMNR, mDNS).why: Put a name to an address from the ARP table, a log or a firewall.

This PC vs my phone.tag: The same checks from this PC and from your linked phone, side by side.
This PC vs my phone.what: Asks your linked phone (Your phone page) to time the same sites and the internet that this PC times, then lays the two results next to each other.
This PC vs my phone.why: If only the PC is slow, look at this PC or its Wi-Fi; if both are slow on the same Wi-Fi, it's the network or the provider; if the phone on mobile data is fine, it's your line.

Is it down - from this PC and my phone.what: This PC fetches the site, and your linked phone does the same from its own connection; the verdict says whether it's down for both or only one.
Is it down - from this PC and my phone.why: Down from both: the site, or the whole network. Down only here: this PC, its browser settings or a block on its path.

SSH, SCP and remote commands.what: Fills in the commands for Windows' own OpenSSH (ssh, scp, sftp, ssh-keyscan, ssh-keygen), curl and PowerShell with your host, user and port. Click one to copy it; click the top line to open PowerShell.
SSH, SCP and remote commands.how: Nothing runs from AdeeboMeter and no password is typed or kept here.

Many ports for one service.why: Sign-in, mail or printing often fails on one missing port, not all of them.

labels.25 SMTP|2: Most home providers block port 25 out - use 587.

Every IP behind a name.tag: Does every server behind the name answer?
Every IP behind a name.what: Resolves a name to all its addresses and tries the port on each one.
Every IP behind a name.how: A TCP connection to each address (16 at most).
Every IP behind a name.why: "Works on retry" is often one dead server among several - this finds it.

Remote Desktop reachable?.what: Opens the RDP port and does Remote Desktop's own opening negotiation to see that it really answers and whether it requires sign-in first (NLA).
Remote Desktop reachable?.how: No sign-in and no password - the negotiation stops before that.
Remote Desktop reachable?.why: Tells "port blocked" from "Remote Desktop off" from "works".

Active Directory / LDAP reachable?.tag: Can I reach the domain controller?
Active Directory / LDAP reachable?.what: Reads the directory's root (rootDSE) anonymously, as every client does first: domain, server name, functional level and its clock - then checks LDAPS, the global catalog and Kerberos ports.
Active Directory / LDAP reachable?.how: Anonymous read, no password; plain BER over TCP 389.
Active Directory / LDAP reachable?.why: Sign-in and Group Policy need the DC and a clock within 5 minutes of it.

DNS answer compare.tag: Does my DNS say the same as another?
DNS answer compare.what: Asks your DNS server and one you name (an IP or a DoH address) for the same name and compares the addresses.
DNS answer compare.why: A site that fails only here may get a different, wrong answer from this network's DNS.

Before / after snapshot.what: Takes a snapshot of adapter, addresses, gateway, DNS, VPN, proxy, MTU and response times; run it again after one change (VPN on, dock, Wi-Fi to cable) and it lists exactly what changed.
Before / after snapshot.how: Read from Windows and what AdeeboMeter already measures; kept in memory until AdeeboMeter closes.
Before / after snapshot.why: "It breaks when I connect the VPN" - this shows what the VPN actually changed.

Compare two saved results (two PCs).tag: Why does it work on the other PC?
Compare two saved results (two PCs).what: Reads two results saved from AdeeboMeter (one from each PC) and lists the lines that differ.
Compare two saved results (two PCs).why: The difference between a working and a broken PC is usually one line - a DNS answer, a route, a proxy.

What changed on my server?.tag: A server's DNS, open ports and certificate, compared with the last time you checked.
What changed on my server?.what: Looks up the server's addresses and mail and name records, knocks on a few common ports and reads its certificate, then compares with the earlier runs kept on this PC.
What changed on my server?.why: When something broke overnight, the line that changed is usually the cause.

Service board - my hosts and ports.tag: Your own hosts and ports, up or down right now.
Service board - my hosts and ports.what: Opens a TCP connection to each host and port you list (or your pinned sites), times it and closes it - nothing else is sent.
Service board - my hosts and ports.why: A quick morning check of the things you look after; set minutes to keep watching in the background.

Uptime report.tag: How much of the time the internet was there, over the last days.
Uptime report.what: Reads AdeeboMeter's own History - nothing new is measured.
Uptime report.why: A number to show your provider, with the outages listed by time.

Certificate calendar.tag: When the certificates on your sites run out.
Certificate calendar.what: Reads each site's certificate over TLS and sorts them by days left.
Certificate calendar.why: Catch the one that didn't renew before visitors see a warning.

My sites.how: One DNS question, one TCP connection and one TLS handshake per site.
My sites.why: Your own short watchlist, checked in seconds.

labels.intranet.example.net|2: Only reachable on the company network or VPN.

Shared folders on a PC or NAS (SMB).tag: What does this PC or NAS share?
Shared folders on a PC or NAS (SMB).what: Lists the shared folders and printers on a PC or NAS, as Windows would show them to your account.
Shared folders on a PC or NAS (SMB).how: Windows' own share listing (NetShareEnum) with your credentials; nothing is opened or read.
Shared folders on a PC or NAS (SMB).why: Find the right share name, or see whether access is denied for your account.

Services that failed to start (7 days).what: Reads 7 days of the System log for services that failed to start, timed out or stopped unexpectedly, grouped by service.
Services that failed to start (7 days).how: Windows' own event log, read as you.
Services that failed to start (7 days).why: A VPN, antivirus or network service that fails at start-up explains a lot of "sometimes" problems.

Speed test.tag: How fast is my internet right now - to the city I choose?
Speed test.what: Downloads (and, where the server allows, uploads) for about 8 seconds each and pings that server while the line is full - so you see the speed and whether calls and games would stutter while someone downloads. Pick the server: Auto (Cloudflare's nearest data centre, download and upload), or a city from Vultr's or OVHcloud's public test files (download only), or your own file URL. "Find the closest
Speed test.how: Only when you press it - never in the background. Nothing about you is sent; the server only sees an ordinary download. Capped at 400 MB down and 100 MB up. A few providers' test files have no HTTPS - then the test data comes over plain HTTP and the result says so. Your own servers go in speedservers.txt in AdeeboMeter's data folder: server|id|provider|city|download URL|upload URL. In the Toolbox,
Speed test.why: "Is it my internet?" usually starts here. Testing to a city also answers "is it slow everywhere, or only to Europe?" - and the ping while the line is busy matters as much as the speed.

Side by side: Wi-Fi vs cable (a game).tag: Is the cable really better? Is my PC the problem?
Side by side: Wi-Fi vs cable (a game).what: Measures a game's servers 30 times each and saves the run under a name you choose - Wi-Fi, Cable, Laptop. Switch the connection (or run it on another PC) and run again: every saved run shows side by side, with which one is steadier, loses fewer packets and is quicker.
Side by side: Wi-Fi vs cable (a game).how: One probe a second to each of the game's servers (up to 8), the same way the Gamer Zone measures them. Up to 4 runs per game are kept on this PC. To compare two PCs, copy the run on one and paste it into the name box on the other - it's one line of numbers, nothing else.
Side by side: Wi-Fi vs cable (a game).why: "Use a cable" is the first advice every gamer gets. This shows whether it actually helps on your setup - and whether one PC (drivers, background apps) is the problem rather than the line.

Why didn't this PC join the network?.what: Walks the steps a PC takes to get online - link, network sign-in (802.1X), an address from DHCP, the router, names (DNS), the internet - and says where the evidence ends.
Why didn't this PC join the network?.how: Reads the adapter, Windows' own sign-in log and what AdeeboMeter already measured. Nothing is sent.
Why didn't this PC join the network?.why: "No network" has six possible places to break. The first broken step is the one to fix - the later ones can't work until it does.

labels.Verdict|2: Next: open 802.1X failure decoder for the full timeline.

802.1X failure decoder (timeline).tag: Why did the network sign-in fail?
802.1X failure decoder (timeline).what: Puts Windows' own 802.1X events - Wi-Fi and cable, the last 2 days - on one timeline: started, succeeded, failed, with the reason in plain words, and says where it stopped.
802.1X failure decoder (timeline).how: Reads the WLAN-AutoConfig and Wired-AutoConfig logs, which Windows lets you read without admin rights (a company PC may restrict them - then it says so). Nothing is sent.
802.1X failure decoder (timeline).why: Company networks sign the PC (or you) in before letting any traffic through. When that fails, the PC looks connected but gets nothing - the reason is in these logs, worded for engineers.

DHCP lease replay (from a capture).tag: What happened when the PC asked for an address?
DHCP lease replay (from a capture).what: Reads a capture file and rebuilds each DHCP conversation - Discover, Offer, Request, ACK - with who answered, the options given, the relay and option 82. Finds two DHCP servers answering (a rogue one), no answer at all, refusals (NAK) and what changed between a good and a bad lease.
DHCP lease replay (from a capture).how: Reads a .pcap / .pcapng with AdeeboMeter's own reader - no Wireshark needed, nothing is sent. Capture with filter udp port 67 or udp port 68 while the PC connects.
DHCP lease replay (from a capture).why: Most "connected, no internet" cases at the edge are DHCP: no server on the VLAN, a missing relay, a full pool or a rogue router handing out wrong addresses.

IPv6 RA replay (from a capture).what: Reads a capture file and lists every IPv6 router announcing itself: its prefixes, lifetimes, flags (DHCPv6 or not), MTU and DNS - and flags a second, unexpected router.
IPv6 RA replay (from a capture).how: Reads a .pcap / .pcapng with AdeeboMeter's own reader; nothing is sent. Capture for a minute with filter icmpv6.type == 134.
IPv6 RA replay (from a capture).why: A rogue Router Advertisement (a hotspot, a VM host) can quietly send a network's IPv6 traffic the wrong way - sites half-work, or not at all.

labels.fe80::bad|2: Windows may send IPv6 traffic to it. Find the device with this address and turn off its router announcements.

802.1X replay (from a capture).tag: What happened in the network sign-in, frame by frame?
802.1X replay (from a capture).what: Reads a capture file and rebuilds the 802.1X exchange - EAPOL-Start, the switch asking who's there, the identity, the method (PEAP, EAP-TLS, TTLS) and the server's Success or Failure - then says where and why it stopped: no answer from the PC, a method the two sides don't share, a certificate problem or a refusal.
802.1X replay (from a capture).how: Reads a .pcap / .pcapng with AdeeboMeter's own reader; nothing is sent. Capture on the PC's cable port with the filter eapol while it connects. Wi-Fi 802.1X happens inside the radio - capture it on the access point.
802.1X replay (from a capture).why: The Windows log says that sign-in failed; the frames show at which step - the quickest way to tell a PC problem from a switch or RADIUS problem.

labels.Result|2: The server refused - usually a certificate one side doesn't trust.

ICMP error translator.tag: What is this ICMP error telling me?
ICMP error translator.what: Turns ICMP and ICMPv6 error messages into plain words - unreachable, fragmentation needed (with the MTU), TTL exceeded, administratively prohibited - and shows which packet caused each one. Give it a capture file, or just a type/code like 3/4.
ICMP error translator.how: Reads the capture with AdeeboMeter's own reader; nothing is sent.
ICMP error translator.why: Routers explain what went wrong in ICMP - but in numbers. Reading them tells you whether it's a missing route, a firewall, an MTU problem or a closed port.

Certificate chain compare.tag: Does someone re-sign this site on one path?
Certificate chain compare.what: Connects to the same site from two places - VPN on and off, office and home, through the proxy and direct - and compares the certificate chains: fingerprints, issuers and whether Windows trusts them.
Certificate chain compare.how: One TLS handshake per run, nothing else sent. Each run is kept on this PC (fingerprints and names only) so the next run compares with it.
Certificate chain compare.why: A different issuer on one path means something re-signs the encryption: a company proxy doing inspection (expected if IT says so), antivirus, or an interception on a network you don't control.

RADIUS client lab (test account).tag: Does the RADIUS server accept this test account - and what does it send back?
RADIUS client lab (test account).what: Sends one Access-Request (PAP) with a TEST account to a RADIUS server you manage and decodes the answer: Accept, Reject, Challenge or silence, and the attributes returned - VLAN, Session-Timeout, Filter-Id, vendor attributes. Each run is compared with the previous one (before / after a change) and with the last run to another server. Also checks TACACS+ on the same server.
RADIUS client lab (test account).how: The shared secret and password are used for this one request and wiped - never shown, saved, logged or copied. The request carries a Message-Authenticator. This PC must be a client (NAS) on the server.
RADIUS client lab (test account).why: After a policy change, the question is always "what does the server answer now?". This answers it in seconds - from your PC, with the attributes the switch would get.

SMTP delivery path (MX, STARTTLS).tag: Can mail reach this domain, and is it encrypted?
SMTP delivery path (MX, STARTTLS).what: Finds a domain's mail servers (MX), then talks to the top two on port 25: greeting, EHLO, STARTTLS and its certificate - and stops before sending anything.
SMTP delivery path (MX, STARTTLS).how: One DNS question, then a short SMTP conversation that ends with QUIT before MAIL FROM - no message is ever sent. Home providers usually block port 25; then it says so.
SMTP delivery path (MX, STARTTLS).why: When mail bounces or arrives unencrypted, the path - MX, the server's answer, STARTTLS - is where to look first.

Sample captures - good and broken.tag: Learn what good and broken look like.
Sample captures - good and broken.what: Small example captures made by AdeeboMeter: a normal DHCP lease, two DHCP servers, nobody answering, a refused lease, a rogue IPv6 router and common ICMP errors. Each opens here with the replay that explains it, and is saved so you can open the same packets in Wireshark.
Sample captures - good and broken.how: Written on this PC with documentation addresses (192.0.2.x, 2001:db8::) - nothing is captured or sent.
Sample captures - good and broken.why: Seeing the broken pattern once makes it easy to spot in a real capture.

labels.Sample|3: Made by AdeeboMeter - addresses are documentation examples, not real devices.
labels.No ACK for 02:00:5e:10:00:01|1: The Request didn't reach the server, or its answer didn't come back - a relay that forwards one way only, or a firewall.

Trading session tape.tag: A trading day's recording: the line to your broker, minute by minute.
Trading session tape.what: Reads the session AdeeboMeter kept while the broker watch ran - nothing new is measured.
Trading session tape.why: Match a bad fill or a frozen chart with what the line was doing at that minute.

labels.Most of it|1: Your home network was fine each time - note the times and send the Report for my ISP.

Market-open check (GO / HOLD).tag: Is the line to your broker ready before the open?
Market-open check (GO / HOLD).what: Times the connection to your broker, checks this PC's load and the internet, and gives one word: GO or HOLD.
Market-open check (GO / HOLD).why: HOLD before the open means fix the line first - not mid-trade.

labels.Market-open check|1: AdeeboMeter only checks - it never trades, closes or changes anything.
labels.Background|1: Pause it - it can start a big transfer any second.
labels.Clock|1: Order and fill times are stamped by this clock - fix it in Settings > Time > Sync now.

Report for my ISP.tag: The evidence a provider's support desk asks for, ready to send.
Report for my ISP.what: Traces the path to your game's server (or any host), measures every hop at once for 1, 2 or 5 minutes, and compares a second route at the same moment. Adds the hour-of-day loss pattern from the last 7 days, your line details and cable modem levels if the modem shows them, the worst spikes and outages, and a message to paste into the support chat.
Report for my ISP.how: One small ping a second to each hop, from this PC only. Router names come from your DNS server. The cable modem page (192.168.100.1) is read once without logging in. The report is saved as a web page in AdeeboMeter's own folder - open it and Print > Save as PDF to attach it. Internal addresses, hardware addresses and your Wi-Fi name are taken out. A raw CSV of every hop is saved next to it. Who ow
Report for my ISP.why: "It lags in the evenings" gets a script read back to you. "Loss starts at hop 6, inside your network, every evening from 19:00, on this route but not that one" gets passed to the network team - who can fix it or move your traffic.

Quick tidy (you do it, I show where).what: Finds old temp files, the Recycle Bin, low disk space, startup programs, frozen or memory-hungry apps and recent installs, and opens the right Windows screen for each.
Quick tidy (you do it, I show where).how: Reads only; deletes, ends and changes nothing. No registry cleaning, memory boosting or cache wiping - they don't help.
Quick tidy (you do it, I show where).why: Most "PC cleanup" is a few Windows screens you can use yourself.

My keys.what: The keys and certificates AdeeboMeter made or put together for you, each with what it's for and when it expires - and, for each one, Copy public key, Back up private key and Delete.
My keys.how: They live in Windows' own certificate store for your account (Current User › Personal) - no admin needed. Windows protects the private keys; AdeeboMeter never writes one to a file of its own, except a password-protected backup when you ask.
My keys.why: A key you can find, back up and share safely is the start of encrypting files, mTLS clients and lab servers.

New key.tag: Make a key of your own.
New key.what: Makes a key and keeps it in Windows for your account: for files encrypted to you (default), a server, or an mTLS client. For files you choose the type: standard (RSA 3072 - .p7m files that open in other tools too) or P-384 (elliptic curve, the strongest - .adeebo files only AdeeboMeter opens; its public key travels as a .adeebokey file).
New key.how: Offline. The key never leaves the PC unless you back it up.
New key.why: Others can only encrypt files for you once you have a key and send them its public part.

labels.Made|0: Next: Copy public key (in My keys) and send it to anyone who'll encrypt files for you.

Generate a CSR.tag: Ask your CA for a certificate.
Generate a CSR.what: Makes a certificate signing request for one of My keys (or a new key made now) with the DNS names and IP addresses you list as Subject Alternative Names, and saves the .csr to send to your CA.
Generate a CSR.how: Offline. The private key stays in Windows. When the certificate comes back, Check certificate and key puts the two together.
Generate a CSR.why: Every CA starts from a CSR - and a wrong or missing name in it is the most common reason a new certificate doesn't work.

Create a self-signed certificate.tag: A certificate for the lab, in one step.
Create a self-signed certificate.what: Presets: Local HTTPS (localhost and the names you give, 397 days), Lab server (2 years) and mTLS client. The key goes into My keys; the public certificate is saved to copy to the server or client.
Create a self-signed certificate.how: Offline. Nothing is ever added to Windows' trusted roots - you decide where to trust it.
Create a self-signed certificate.why: Lab servers, test portals and mTLS tests need a certificate today, not after a CA ticket.

labels.Trust|1: Browsers and clients will warn until you add this certificate to their trusted list.

Check certificate and key.tag: Does this certificate belong to my key?
Check certificate and key.what: Reads the certificate your CA sent back and finds which of My keys it belongs to - or says none does. Type yes to put them together in My keys, ready to back up as a .pfx.
Check certificate and key.how: Offline: compares the public key inside the certificate with each of your keys.
Check certificate and key.why: "The certificate doesn't match the private key" stops many server installs; this tells you before you get there.

Compare file vs live server.tag: Is the server really using the new certificate?
Compare file vs live server.what: Connects once to the server and compares what it presents with the certificate you meant to deploy, then lists the intermediates it sends and whether Windows trusts the chain.
Compare file vs live server.how: One TLS handshake to the server you type - nothing else.
Compare file vs live server.why: After a certificate renewal the old one often stays loaded, or an intermediate is missing - users find out when it expires.

labels.Different|2: The new one isn't deployed yet, or the service wasn't restarted.

Recipients (their public keys).what: The public keys of people you encrypt files for. Add one from the .cer (standard) or .adeebokey (EC P-384, AdeeboMeter only) they send you and give it a name; you'll pick them by that name in Encrypt a file.
Recipients (their public keys).how: Saved as .cer or .adeebokey files in AdeeboMeter's data folder - public information only. Check the fingerprint with them by phone once.
Recipients (their public keys).why: Encrypting for someone's own key means no code to pass around - only they can open it.

Encrypt a file.tag: Send a file only the right person can open.
Encrypt a file.what: Two ways. Share with a code: makes a .adeebo file and a random 24-character code - send the file, give the code another way (by phone). For a recipient: their key decides the format - a standard RSA key gives a .p7m (CMS / S/MIME, AES-256) that also opens in OpenSSL or Outlook-compatible tools; an EC P-384 key (the strongest choice) gives a .adeebo that only AdeeboMeter opens. Optionally also for
Encrypt a file.how: Offline. .adeebo: PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 rounds), AES-256 and an HMAC-SHA256 check, so a changed file is refused. The code is shown once and never saved. The original file isn't changed.
Encrypt a file.why: Email isn't private. A file encrypted this way stays private wherever it travels.

labels.The code|1: Give it another way than the file - read it out on the phone, or send it by text. (In a real run this is a fresh random code.)

Open an encrypted file.what: Opens a .adeebo file with its code, or a .p7m made for one of your keys - Windows finds the right key. The opened file is saved next to the encrypted one.
Open an encrypted file.how: Offline. A .adeebo file is checked before anything is decrypted: a wrong code or a changed file is refused, never half-opened.
Open an encrypted file.why: The other half of Encrypt a file.

Inspect a certificate file.what: Reads a certificate file (or pasted PEM, or a whole chain) and shows subject, issuer, dates, SAN names, key, signature, fingerprints and chain order.
Inspect a certificate file.how: On this PC only; revocation isn't checked (that needs the internet).
Inspect a certificate file.why: Check a certificate before you install it or send it on.

labels.Valid|0: Outside these dates every app refuses it.
labels.Key|3: The public half of the key pair - the server proves it holds the private half.
labels.Names|3: The names it is valid for.
labels.Is it a CA?|3: CA:true means it vouches for others; a site's own certificate should say no.

Chain check (the ladder of trust).tag: The ladder of trust, link by link.
Chain check (the ladder of trust).what: Draws a certificate's chain as a ladder - root at the top, your certificate at the bottom - and marks each link: who signed it, is the signature real, is the signer allowed to sign, are the dates right, is a middle certificate missing.
Chain check (the ladder of trust).how: All on this PC: the files you give, then Windows' own certificate stores. Nothing is fetched from the internet (revocation only if you switch it on in Settings).
Chain check (the ladder of trust).why: "The site works in Chrome but not in my app" is very often a missing middle certificate.

labels.✗ root|2: a root this PC doesn't trust (not in Windows' trusted roots).
labels.✓ middle|0: Signed by the one above, and allowed to sign the one below.

HTTPS check.tag: How a site's padlock is built.
HTTPS check.what: One site, on click: the TLS version, the cipher in four plain parts (key agreement, server's key, encryption, hash), whether the name matches, days to expiry, the chain as the server sends it, and HTTPS inspection on the way.
HTTPS check.how: Two short handshakes and no HTTP request: one by Windows (what your apps get) and one TLS 1.2 hello that reads the certificates exactly as the server sends them. If the certificate's dates look wrong, your clock is compared too.
HTTPS check.why: Name mismatch, expired, a missing middle certificate, a wrong clock, an old TLS-only server - each has a different fix.

labels.www.example.com:443|0: Two short handshakes, no HTTP request.
labels.Key agreement|3: A fresh secret for every session (forward secrecy): a key stolen later can't open today's traffic.
labels.Server's key|3: A small, fast elliptic-curve key proves who the server is.
labels.Encryption|3: Locks the data and seals it, so any change on the way is caught.
labels.Hash|3: Mixes the keys and checks the handshake wasn't tampered with.
labels.✗ missing|2: The server should send it with its own certificate.

Check a PFX / P12.what: Opens a PFX with its password and shows each certificate, whether the private key is there and usable, and whether the chain is complete.
Check a PFX / P12.how: In memory only (an ephemeral key set); the key is never exported, shown or saved, and the password isn't kept.
Check a PFX / P12.why: Most certificate installs that fail are a PFX without its key or without its intermediates.

Decode a CSR.tag: What does this request ask for?
Decode a CSR.what: Reads a certificate signing request and shows the subject, the SAN names, the key type and size and the signature algorithm.
Decode a CSR.why: Catch a missing SAN name or a weak key before the CA issues the wrong certificate.

Convert a certificate (PEM / DER).what: Writes the certificate in the other form (PEM text or DER binary) as a new file next to the original - never over it.
Convert a certificate (PEM / DER).how: Certificates only; a file holding a private key is refused.
Convert a certificate (PEM / DER).why: Network gear, Linux and Windows each want a different form of the same certificate.

Hash a file and compare.what: Works out SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 of a file at once and compares them with the hash you paste from the download page.
Hash a file and compare.how: Reads the file locally; nothing is sent.
Hash a file and compare.why: A damaged or swapped download - firmware especially - fails the comparison.

Decode Base64 or a JWT.what: Decodes Base64 (or Base64url) to text or bytes with a hint about what they are, or a JWT's header and claims with its issue and expiry times.
Decode Base64 or a JWT.how: On this PC only. A JWT's signature is not checked.
Decode Base64 or a JWT.why: Read a token's claims or expiry, or an encoded blob from a log or config.

Certificate commands (certutil, openssl).what: Lists the everyday certificate commands with your file filled in - dump, verify, convert, hash, the certificate stores - and openssl's when it's installed. Click to copy.
Certificate commands (certutil, openssl).how: Nothing runs from here; exporting private keys is left out on purpose.
Certificate commands (certutil, openssl).why: The commands you'd otherwise search for each time.

RADIUS - is the server alive?.what: Sends a Status-Server request (RFC 5997) signed with the shared secret and checks the signed reply.
RADIUS - is the server alive?.why: Tells a dead server from a wrong secret or a missing client entry - without a user account.

TACACS+ - is the server there?.what: Opens TCP 49 three times and times it.
TACACS+ - is the server there?.why: Shows the daemon is listening and reachable through the firewalls.

Neighbours (ARP table).tag: Who this PC has talked to on its network.
Neighbours (ARP table).what: Lists the local devices Windows has a hardware address for - IP, hardware address, the maker or "private address", and virtual routers. Nothing is sent.
Neighbours (ARP table).why: A quick look at who's on your segment, and whether the gateway is a VRRP / HSRP pair.

Your own router (hairpin).tag: Can you reach home through your own public address?
Your own router (hairpin).what: Learns your public address and port through STUN, then sends a packet to your own public address to see if the router loops it back.
Your own router (hairpin).why: Explains why a camera, NAS or game server works from outside but not from home (or the reverse), and shows CGNAT.

labels.Your own address from inside|2: The router doesn't loop traffic back (no NAT hairpin / loopback). From outside it may work - inside, use the local name or 192.168.1.40.

Ping sweep.what: Pings every address in your own subnet (up to 254), then names makers from the hardware address.
Ping sweep.why: Find the printer, the camera, or the device that shouldn't be there.

Wi-Fi roams and drops (24 h).tag: Every access-point hop in the last 24 hours.
Wi-Fi roams and drops (24 h).what: The Wi-Fi events AdeeboMeter has seen today in order - roams (from which access point to which), drops, channel changes and signal falls - with back-and-forth roams within two minutes marked.
Wi-Fi roams and drops (24 h).how: From the events AdeeboMeter already recorded; nothing new is measured.
Wi-Fi roams and drops (24 h).why: A laptop that ping-pongs between two access points of equal strength stutters calls even with full bars.

DHCP lease and IPv6 lifetimes.tag: Your address lease: when it renews and runs out.
DHCP lease and IPv6 lifetimes.what: The lease Windows holds now - address, DHCP server, when it was obtained, renews (T1), rebinds (T2) and expires, and the router, DNS and domain it handed out - plus where each IPv6 address came from and how long it stays.
DHCP lease and IPv6 lifetimes.how: Reads Windows' own record of the lease (no admin, nothing sent).
DHCP lease and IPv6 lifetimes.why: Drops at the same time every few hours are often a lease that can't renew. A 169.254 address means no DHCP server answered at all.

Wake-on-LAN.tag: Wake a PC on your network.
Wake-on-LAN.what: Sends one magic packet to the hardware address you type.
Wake-on-LAN.why: Handy for a home server or a desktop you left asleep.

Subnet calculator.tag: CIDR, masks and ranges - IPv4 and IPv6.
Subnet calculator.why: Network, broadcast, usable range, wildcard mask, binary; IPv6 expanded and compressed; is this IP inside? Checks a gateway too - outside the subnet, the network or broadcast address, a mask that disagrees - and says what to use instead. Leave the address empty to check this PC's own.

Packet stack and MTU.tag: What fits in one packet - through VPNs, PPPoE, VLANs and labels.
Packet stack and MTU.what: Adds up the headers of each layer you list, top to bottom, against the link MTU. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Packet stack and MTU.why: Gives the biggest TCP segment (MSS), the MTU to set inside a tunnel, the size on the wire, how much of the line carries data, and whether a given size splits.

VLSM planner.tag: Split one block into subnets of the sizes you need.
VLSM planner.what: Biggest first, each on its own boundary, with gateway and broadcast. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
VLSM planner.why: Shows each subnet's range, gateway, broadcast and spare room, and what's left of the block.

Bandwidth and transfer time.tag: How long a download takes, what speed you need, bits vs bytes.
Bandwidth and transfer time.what: Any two of size, speed and time give the third. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Bandwidth and transfer time.why: Also converts the speed (Mbps, MB/s, per hour) and shows how many full-size packets a second it means.

Decimal, hex and binary.tag: One number in decimal, hex, binary - and as an address, mask, MAC or DSCP.
Decimal, hex and binary.what: Reads 200, 0xC8, 0b11001000, C8h, an IPv4 address or a MAC. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Decimal, hex and binary.why: Shows the same value every way a network engineer meets it.

Wildcard mask.tag: Mask, prefix and wildcard - one from the other.
Wildcard mask.what: Turns 255.255.252.0, /22 or 0.0.3.255 into the other two, with the block size and an ACL line. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Wildcard mask.why: Says how many addresses the block holds and spots a mask with gaps.

IPv6 prefix split.tag: Cut an IPv6 prefix into smaller ones.
IPv6 prefix split.what: Splits a /48 into /56s, /64s or a number of pieces, and lists the first and last. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
IPv6 prefix split.why: Shows how many LAN-sized /64s each piece holds.

BDP and TCP window.tag: How much is in flight, and the window to fill a link.
BDP and TCP window.what: Speed × round trip gives the bytes in flight - the TCP window a single stream needs. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
BDP and TCP window.why: Shows the most one stream gets with a given window: why long links feel slow.

Bits, bytes and units.what: Mbps and MB/s, GB and GiB, bits and bytes, minutes and seconds. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Bits, bytes and units.why: Explains why Windows shows less space than the box says.

LTE and 5G throughput.tag: Peak speed of an LTE or 5G NR carrier.
LTE and 5G throughput.what: Bandwidth, MIMO layers and modulation give the peak, using the formula in 3GPP TS 38.306 for NR. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
LTE and 5G throughput.why: Also gives a realistic range - cells are shared and signals aren't perfect.

Wi-Fi speed by channel width.tag: Link rate for a Wi-Fi generation, width and streams.
Wi-Fi speed by channel width.what: Data subcarriers × bits per symbol × streams for Wi-Fi 4 to 7, at the top MCS. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Wi-Fi speed by channel width.why: Shows what you'll really get, and when a narrower channel wins.

Link budget (Wi-Fi, microwave).tag: Will a radio link reach, and with how much margin?
Link budget (Wi-Fi, microwave).what: Transmit power plus antenna gains minus free-space loss, against the receiver's sensitivity. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Link budget (Wi-Fi, microwave).why: Also gives the Fresnel zone to keep clear of trees and roofs.

RAID capacity.tag: Usable space and how many disks it survives.
RAID capacity.what: RAID 0, 1, 5, 6 or 10 with your disk count and size. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
RAID capacity.why: Shows TB and the TiB Windows shows, and reminds you RAID isn't a backup.

Backup and restore time.tag: How long a full copy and a nightly change take.
Backup and restore time.what: Data and link speed at a realistic 70%, plus the daily change. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Backup and restore time.why: Warns when a nightly backup won't finish before morning.

UPS runtime.tag: How long the UPS keeps things running.
UPS runtime.what: Battery energy (Wh, or volts and amp-hours) × efficiency ÷ load. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
UPS runtime.why: Allows for battery age - the label number is the best case.

Uptime and downtime (SLA).what: Uptime to downtime per year, month, week and day - or the other way round. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Uptime and downtime (SLA).why: Also shows what two parts in a row give.

When does storage fill up?.tag: Months until the disks are full.
When does storage fill up?.what: Size now and growth (a % or a fixed amount) against the capacity. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
When does storage fill up?.why: Says when you hit 80% - the time to order more.

Streaming bitrate and upload.tag: The bitrate for a resolution and frame rate.
Streaming bitrate and upload.what: Pixels × frames × bits per pixel for H.264, HEVC or AV1, plus audio. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Streaming bitrate and upload.why: Says the upload you need with headroom, and the data an hour.

Monthly data use.tag: How many GB a month video, calls and games use.
Monthly data use.what: Hours a day of each, at the figures the big services publish. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Monthly data use.why: Says whether it fits a capped plan.

Is my plan fast enough?.tag: Enough speed for everyone at once?
Is my plan fast enough?.what: Adds up what each person is doing (4K, calls, games, streams) against your plan. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Is my plan fast enough?.why: Checks the upload too - calls and streams break up first.

E1 and T1 timeslots.tag: Bandwidth of E1 and T1 timeslots.
E1 and T1 timeslots.what: 64 kbps per timeslot; E1 is 32, T1 is 24 plus framing. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
E1 and T1 timeslots.why: Also the robbed-bit 56k case and how many calls fit.

Jitter buffer size.tag: How big the voice jitter buffer should be.
Jitter buffer size.what: About 1.5 × the delay variation, in whole packets. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Jitter buffer size.why: Estimates mouth-to-ear delay against the 150 ms target.

Currency converter.tag: An amount from one currency to another, at the Bank of Canada's rate.
Currency converter.what: Through the Canadian dollar, at the day's indicative rate the Trading page keeps - then what a bank's markup leaves you. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Currency converter.why: An amount from one currency to another, at the Bank of Canada's rate.

Profit, loss and break-even.tag: Profit or loss on a trade, after fees.
Profit, loss and break-even.what: Commission each way and a currency fee, and the sell price that only covers the fees. Not advice. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Profit, loss and break-even.why: Profit or loss on a trade, after fees.

Position size from risk.tag: How many shares fit the risk you'll accept.
Position size from risk.what: Account × risk % ÷ (entry - stop). A stop isn't guaranteed - prices can jump past it. Not advice. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Position size from risk.why: How many shares fit the risk you'll accept.

Average cost of buying in steps.tag: Your average price after several buys.
Average cost of buying in steps.what: Total paid ÷ total shares. Not advice. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Average cost of buying in steps.why: Your average price after several buys.

Compound growth.tag: What a start amount and monthly additions grow to at a steady rate.
Compound growth.what: Monthly compounding; real returns go up and down. Not advice. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Compound growth.why: What a start amount and monthly additions grow to at a steady rate.

A fall and the rise to get back.what: Percentages work on different bases going down and up. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.

Is my connection fast enough to trade?.tag: How far a price typically moves while your order travels.
Is my connection fast enough to trade?.what: One standard deviation of a day's move, scaled to your round trip. Your reaction time matters far more. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Is my connection fast enough to trade?.why: How far a price typically moves while your order travels.

Commodity units.tag: Barrels, gallons and litres; troy ounces and grams; bushels and tonnes; MMBtu and GJ.
Commodity units.what: Bushels are volumes: wheat and soybeans weigh 60 lb, corn 56 lb. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Commodity units.why: Barrels, gallons and litres; troy ounces and grams; bushels and tonnes; MMBtu and GJ.

Futures contract value.tag: What one contract controls, its tick and a $1 move.
Futures contract value.what: CME contract sizes and ticks. Futures run on margin. Not advice. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Futures contract value.why: What one contract controls, its tick and a $1 move.

Commodity price per unit.tag: A price per barrel or ounce, per litre or gram, in Canadian dollars.
Commodity price per unit.what: Uses the Bank of Canada's US dollar rate. The raw commodity only - taxes and refining come on top. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Commodity price per unit.why: A price per barrel or ounce, per litre or gram, in Canadian dollars.

Ticks behind in a game.tag: How late you see the game: half your ping plus the game's smoothing.
Ticks behind in a game.what: At 64 Hz one tick is 15.6 ms; games add 2 ticks of interpolation on purpose. Pure arithmetic, nothing sent.
Ticks behind in a game.why: How late you see the game: half your ping plus the game's smoothing.

What changed when it broke?.tag: Everything that changed around the moment it broke.
What changed when it broke?.what: Network events AdeeboMeter noted, sleep and wake, Windows updates, new drivers and installed programs - in order, with the closest change before the break named as the first suspect.
What changed when it broke?.how: From AdeeboMeter's own timeline (History keeps it past two hours) and Windows' System log; nothing is sent.
What changed when it broke?.why: If something changed just before, undo that first; if nothing changed on this PC, the cause is outside it.

Is this Wi-Fi OK to use? (hotel, cafe).tag: Hotel, cafe or airport Wi-Fi: safe enough, or use a VPN?
Is this Wi-Fi OK to use? (hotel, cafe).what: Checks the Wi-Fi lock (open, WEP, WPA2, WPA3), a sign-in page in the way, DNS that answers for names that don't exist, whether Windows treats it as Public, how many other guests reach you, and whether someone opens your HTTPS.
Is this Wi-Fi OK to use? (hotel, cafe).how: Two requests go out when you press Run: Windows' own internet test and one HTTPS connection to microsoft.com. Everything else is read from this PC.
Is this Wi-Fi OK to use? (hotel, cafe).why: A clear yes or no before you sign in to anything.

DNS race - which server is fastest here.tag: Which DNS server answers fastest from here.
DNS race - which server is fastest here.what: Asks your DNS, your router and a few public ones the same names - known ones (cached) and made-up ones (it has to go and find out) - and compares the typical times.
DNS race - which server is fastest here.how: About 30 small questions per server, only when you press Run.
DNS race - which server is fastest here.why: Slow DNS makes every new site wait. Speed isn't everything: a company PC must keep its own DNS.

Devices on this network.tag: Every device seen here, kept over time - with your own labels.
Devices on this network.what: From the ARP table AdeeboMeter already reads every ten minutes: address, hardware address, maker, first and last seen. Give one a name with  aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff = Living room TV.
Devices on this network.how: Nothing is scanned for it; a Ping sweep fills it in faster. Kept on this PC only.
Devices on this network.why: Know what's yours, and notice what isn't.

Drivers, device problems and USB history.tag: Devices with a problem, old network drivers, and every USB device seen.
Drivers, device problems and USB history.what: Each device's Windows problem code in plain words with the one thing to try, network / Bluetooth / USB drivers with their date, and USB devices by when they last came and went.
Drivers, device problems and USB history.how: Read from Windows' Plug and Play list - no admin, nothing changed.
Drivers, device problems and USB history.why: Old network drivers cause drops; a USB device with a problem code says why it won't work.

labels.USB Receiver|2: The classic USB failure: try another port and cable (a hub without power often causes it); then update the driver.

Why isn't my USB device working?.tag: Not detected, not working or keeps disconnecting - why.
Why isn't my USB device working?.what: Windows' problem code for the device in plain words, when it last dropped out and came back, USB power saving and battery saver, and for a USB network adapter or phone tethering whether the link is really up. Ends with a verdict and one thing to try.
Why isn't my USB device working?.how: Read from Windows' Plug and Play list - no admin, nothing changed.
Why isn't my USB device working?.why: Most USB trouble is the cable, the port, power or the driver - this says which.

labels.USB Headset|1: If you didn't unplug it then, it dropped out by itself: a loose or long cable, a worn port, or not enough power (a hub without its own power supply, or a front-panel port). Try a port on the back of the PC, straight in.

Why is my game lagging?.tag: Lag, stutter, rubber banding, high ping - where it starts.
Why is my game lagging?.what: Splits the path into this PC to the router, the router to your provider, and on to the game's server, from the pings AdeeboMeter already sends, and checks what else is happening: an upload, a busy PC, recent spikes. Ends with which part is at fault and what to do.
Why is my game lagging?.how: No new traffic: it reads the pings already running (the Gamer Zone's for the game server).
Why is my game lagging?.why: Wi-Fi, provider, server or the PC itself - each has a different fix.

What did Windows Update break?.tag: Did an update or a new driver make the connection worse?
What did Windows Update break?.what: Every update and driver installed in the last 14 days, each with your ping and outages for the three days before and the three days after it, from AdeeboMeter's History. Names the one where things got worse - and whether it's still like that.
What did Windows Update break?.how: Windows' own install log and AdeeboMeter's History; nothing is sent. Needs History on for the comparison.
What did Windows Update break?.why: A lasting slowdown that starts the day after an update is worth undoing to test. It says "started after", never "caused by" - a provider can have a bad week too.

labels.Verdict|2: It started then - that's not proof it's the cause (your provider can have a bad week too). To test it: Settings › Windows Update › Update history › Uninstall updates. If it gets better, that was it.

Would a GPN (ping booster) help me?.tag: Paid ping reducers re-route your game traffic - would it help you?
Would a GPN (ping booster) help me?.what: Reads where this run's spikes started (home, provider, past it), traces the way to the game's best region and times each router five times. Says plainly whether a GPN could help - and names the hop where the delay starts.
Would a GPN (ping booster) help me?.how: About 100 pings to the routers on the way, once, when you press Run.
Would a GPN (ping booster) help me?.why: A GPN can't fix Wi-Fi, a busy PC or the game's own server. Many people pay for one that can't help.

labels.Would a GPN help?|0: The delay starts at hop 6 (198.51.100.40), between your provider and the game. A GPN takes another road around it.
labels.Spikes this run|3: From the Gamer Zone's own pings.

After-stream report.tag: A stream's recording: when it dipped and why.
After-stream report.what: Reads the stream session AdeeboMeter kept - nothing new is measured.
After-stream report.why: Each dip next to what the line and this PC were doing then.

labels.Most of it|1: A cable, or the 5 GHz band closer to the router, ends most of these.

OBS link - why frames drop.tag: Asks OBS on this PC why it drops frames.
OBS link - why frames drop.what: Connects to OBS's own WebSocket on this PC and reads its stream statistics - the password is used once and never saved.
OBS link - why frames drop.why: Dropped frames are the network; skipped or lagged frames are this PC.

labels.OBS link|1: Only asks OBS; never starts, stops or changes anything.
labels.Dropped|2: The upload can't keep up: lower the bitrate (Ready to stream? suggests a safe one), use a cable, or pause uploads.

Ready to stream? (go-live check).tag: Can your line carry your stream's bitrate right now?
Ready to stream? (go-live check).what: Checks this PC's load, the upload and the path to the streaming service's ingest server against the bitrate you plan.
Ready to stream? (go-live check).why: Go live only when the upload has room to spare - about 1.5 times the bitrate.

labels.Go-live check|1: AdeeboMeter only checks - it never changes OBS or closes anything.
labels.Upload in use now|1: Something on this PC is already uploading (a backup, cloud sync) - it competes with the stream.

Ready to play? (pre-match checklist).tag: What could spoil the match right now?
Ready to play? (pre-match checklist).what: Wi-Fi or cable and the signal, your router and internet right now, this PC's own traffic, updaters and sync apps that are running, CPU and memory hogs, and the best server for your game.
Ready to play? (pre-match checklist).how: Reads what AdeeboMeter already measures and the list of running programs. Nothing is closed for you.
Ready to play? (pre-match checklist).why: One look before you queue beats finding out mid-match.

labels.Ready to play?|1: AdeeboMeter only suggests - it never closes a program for you.
labels.Connection|1: Weak. A cable is the single best fix for lag; or move closer to the router.
labels.Background|1: Pause it before you play - it can start a download any second.

Best time to play.tag: Which hours your game's server plays best - and worst.
Best time to play.what: Your game's best server, from the Gamer Zone's history, by weekday and hour: the three best and three worst hours, and whether evenings are worse.
Best time to play.how: Gamer Zone history only (kept on this PC). Nothing is sent.
Best time to play.why: Peak hours on your provider's network are real; now you know yours.

labels.Evenings|1: Peak time on your provider's network.

Which game plays best right now?.tag: Every game you watch, ranked by its best server right now.
Which game plays best right now?.what: The last minute of pings to each watched game's best region, ranked by ping, loss and jitter.
Which game plays best right now?.how: Pings the Gamer Zone already sends. Nothing new.

Console mode (PlayStation, Xbox, Switch).tag: Lag on a console: is it the console's link, home, or the internet?
Console mode (PlayStation, Xbox, Switch).what: Pings the console from this PC once a second, and reads your router, the internet check and the game's region at the same time - then says which leg is off.
Console mode (PlayStation, Xbox, Switch).how: One small ping a second to the console, for the seconds you choose. The game region is timed every 5 s.
Console mode (PlayStation, Xbox, Switch).why: Console players have no tools for this.

labels.PC → console|1: Your home network to the console - includes the console's Wi-Fi.
labels.Fortnite|3: The cloud region the game runs in, timed from this PC.

Your month on the network.tag: A month in one page: smooth minutes, outages, delay, data.
Your month on the network.what: How smooth the month was, outages and their minutes, the usual delay, data used, the best and worst day, rush hour, the laggiest game - and a comparison with the month before.
Your month on the network.how: From History (one line a minute, on this PC). Nothing is sent.
Your month on the network.why: Know whether things are getting better or worse - with numbers.

labels.Smooth|1: A minute counts as rough when AdeeboMeter's verdict was a problem.
labels.Outages|1: The internet check got no answer at all.
labels.Data|3: Counted from Windows' own counters, all networks.
labels.Worst day|1: Open it in the Time machine to see what happened.
labels.Rush hour|3: The slowest hour of the week on your own network.

Six months on your network (to share).tag: Half a year in one review - and a file to keep or send.
Six months on your network (to share).what: The same numbers as the monthly review over six months, then month by month. Saves an HTML page you can open, print or send (names and addresses left out). Kept for 180 days, History writes this review by itself before the oldest days roll off.
Six months on your network (to share).how: From History on this PC. The review file stays in AdeeboMeter's reports folder until you delete it.
Six months on your network (to share).why: Evidence over months for your provider, landlord or IT - or just to know.

Wi-Fi rush hour.tag: Your network's slowest hour on each day of the week.
Wi-Fi rush hour.what: Router delay by weekday and hour over the last four weeks, from History: the slowest hour of each day, and which ones are twice the usual.
Wi-Fi rush hour.how: From History on this PC. Nothing new is measured.
Wi-Fi rush hour.why: Schedule big downloads and updates outside rush hour.

labels.Usual|3: Rush hour is usually when everyone at home - or in the building - is streaming.
labels.Friday|1: 3.5× the usual - your network's rush hour.

How fast is it online after waking?.tag: Seconds from opening the lid to working internet.
How fast is it online after waking?.what: Each time the PC wakes from sleep, AdeeboMeter times how long until the router answers and then DNS. Shows the average, the slowest and day by day.
How fast is it online after waking?.how: Right after waking it pings the router every second until it answers - then back to normal.
How fast is it online after waking?.why: A slow wake is usually Wi-Fi power saving or a slow DHCP renew - both fixable.

labels.Back online after waking|1: Slow wake-ups are usually the Wi-Fi adapter's power saving or a long DHCP renew.

Data cap forecast.tag: At this pace, when do you hit your cap?
Data cap forecast.what: This month's data so far and the pace per day; with a cap set in Settings, the date you'd reach it and how much a day keeps you under.
Data cap forecast.how: Windows' own byte counters, on this PC.
Data cap forecast.why: No surprise bill at the end of the month.

labels.This month so far|3: Counted on this PC from Windows' own counters - other devices on the plan aren't included.
labels.At this pace|1: To stay under: 9.9 GB a day from now.

How long will this download take?.tag: At your real speed - not the advertised one.
How long will this download take?.what: Uses the speed tests you ran (median, and evenings) and the fastest minutes History saw, by hour, to say how long a download of that size takes - and when it'd be fastest.
How long will this download take?.how: From History and your speed tests. Nothing is sent.
How long will this download take?.why: A 50 GB update at 2 am vs 9 pm can be hours apart.

labels.At your measured speed|0: The middle of 4 speed tests you ran in the last 30 days.

Network settings snapshot - what changed.tag: Save your DNS, proxy, hosts and adapter settings - compare later.
Network settings snapshot - what changed.what: Saves each adapter's address, router and DNS servers, DHCP, the proxy and proxy script, and a fingerprint of the hosts file. Later it lists exactly what changed - and how to put each back.

Network settings snapshot - what changed.why: A VPN, an installer or adware can change your DNS or proxy silently. Now you see it.

IPv6 readiness score.tag: Is IPv6 ready here: ready, half-ready, or off?
IPv6 readiness score.what: Five checks: a public IPv6 address, privacy addresses, an IPv6 router, DNS answers with IPv6, and a ping to Cloudflare's IPv6 DNS. One score and the line to fix first.
IPv6 readiness score.how: One DNS question to your own DNS server and one IPv6 ping (skipped when the internet check is off by policy).
IPv6 readiness score.why: IPv6 can mean a shorter path and no shared provider NAT for games and calls.

VPN leak test (IPv4, IPv6, DNS).what: Asks a STUN server which address it sees through the normal route and through your Wi-Fi or cable directly, checks whether IPv6 bypasses the VPN, and whether the VPN sets its own DNS server.

VPN leak test (IPv4, IPv6, DNS).why: A VPN that leaks IPv6 or DNS gives your real address and the sites you visit away.
